items.topic: inference-t7 · Bayesian estimation with a Poisson prior and binomial sampling; posterior distribution and estimator comparison
items.stem: Suppose X|n follows Binomial(n,p), where 0<p<1 is known and n∈{0,1,2,…} is unknown. The prior distribution of n is Poisson with known mean λ>0. Which statements are correct?
statements: The posterior distribution of n is Poisson with a mean different from λ.
If X=0, the posterior distribution of n is Poisson with mean λ(1−p).
Under squared-error loss, the Bayes estimate of n has frequentist bias (λ−n)/2 when p=1/2.
The Bayes estimate of n has larger variance than the unbiased estimator X/p.

A.why: For a general observation X=x, the posterior is n=x+K where K is Poisson(λ(1−p)); it is a shifted Poisson, not generally a Poisson distribution for n itself.

B.why: When x=0, the shift is zero, so n|X=0 is Poisson with mean λ(1−p).

C.why: The posterior mean is x+λ(1−p). Its expectation given n is np+λ(1−p), so the bias is (1−p)(λ−n), equal to (λ−n)/2 when p=1/2.

D.why: The Bayes estimate differs from X only by a constant, so its variance is np(1−p), whereas Var(X/p)=n(1−p)/p. The Bayes estimate has smaller variance for 0<p<1.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 52 (June 2018) on page 26. The supplied answer list on page 63 ends at Question 44, so no printed key is available; the statements are derived directly. The prior mass is P(n)=e^(−λ)λⁿ/n!, and the likelihood is proportional to C(n,x)pˣ(1−p)^(n−x), for n≥x. Put k=n−x. Then the posterior mass is proportional to [λ(1−p)]ᵏ/k!, after removing factors that do not depend on k. Hence n|X=x has the representation x+K, where K~Poisson(λ(1−p)). This is a shifted Poisson distribution, so statement A is false in general. When x=0, the shift disappears and statement B is true. Under squared-error loss, the Bayes estimate is the posterior mean δ(X)=X+λ(1−p). Given the fixed parameter n, E[δ(X)|n]=np+λ(1−p), so its frequentist bias is (1−p)(λ−n). At p=1/2 this is (λ−n)/2, making statement C true. Finally, adding a constant does not change variance, so Var[δ(X)|n]=Var(X|n)=np(1−p). The unbiased estimator X/p has variance n(1−p)/p, which is larger because p<1. Thus statement D is false. The correct combination is B and C, option B. Other-exam relevance: Bayesian estimation, conjugate/mixture distributions, posterior means and frequentist properties of Bayes estimators are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. items.topic: inference-t4 · maximum likelihood for a finite discrete parameter space and mixture densities
items.stem: Let X₁ and X₂ be a random sample from fθ(x)=θφ(x)+(1−θ)(1/2)e^(−|x|), −∞<x<∞, where φ is the standard normal density and θ∈{0,1/2,1}. If the observed values are X₁=0 and X₂=2, what is the maximum-likelihood estimate of θ?
items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 53 (December 2017) on page 27. The supplied answer list on PDF page 64 explicitly gives Question 53 as A. We independently compare the likelihood at the three allowed parameter values and obtain the same result. The likelihood is L(θ)=fθ(0)fθ(2). At θ=0, both observations come from the Laplace component: f₀(0)=1/2 and f₀(2)=e^(−2)/2≈0.067668, giving L(0)≈0.033834. At θ=1/2, f(0)=[φ(0)+1/2]/2≈0.449471 and f(2)=[φ(2)+e^(−2)/2]/2≈0.060829, giving L(1/2)≈0.02734. At θ=1, the likelihood is φ(0)φ(2)≈0.02154. Since L(0) is largest among the three permitted values, the MLE is θ̂=0, option A. items.topic: inference-t4 · unbiased estimation of a variance parameter under Poisson and normal models
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from a distribution with density or mass function fθ, and let S²=(1/(n−1))Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)². For which of the following models is S² an unbiased estimator of θ?
statements: X has a Poisson distribution with mean θ>0.
X has a normal distribution N(0,θ), where θ>0.
X has an exponential distribution with mean θ>0.
X has an exponential distribution with rate θ>0.

A.why: For a Poisson(θ) variable, Var(X)=θ. The usual sample variance with denominator n−1 is unbiased for the population variance, so E(S²)=θ.

B.why: For N(0,θ), the variance is θ. Again E(S²)=Var(X)=θ.

C.why: An exponential distribution with mean θ has variance θ², so E(S²)=θ², not θ in general.

D.why: An exponential distribution with rate θ has variance 1/θ², not θ in general.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 56 (December 2017), page 29. The supplied answer key on page 64 lists A,B. The sample variance S²=(1/(n−1))Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)² is unbiased for the population variance: E(S²)=Var(X). Therefore, check the variance of each proposed distribution, not merely its mean. (A) If X~Poisson(θ), then E(X)=Var(X)=θ, so E(S²)=θ. (B) If X~N(0,θ), the second parameter is the variance, so Var(X)=θ and E(S²)=θ. (C) An exponential distribution parameterised by its mean θ has Var(X)=θ², so this does not estimate θ unbiasedly. (D) An exponential distribution with rate θ has Var(X)=1/θ², again not θ. Thus the true statements are A and B, option A. The scan's wording is singular, but two listed models satisfy the condition; the bank preserves both mathematically correct choices and marks the item as multi-answer. items.topic: inference-t4 · consistency, variance comparison and sufficiency for independent heteroscedastic normal observations
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be independent, with Xᵢ~N(μ,i), i=1,…,n. Define X̄ₙ=(1/n)ΣXᵢ and Sₙ=[Σ(Xᵢ/i)]/[Σ(1/i)]. Which statements are true?
statements: E(X̄ₙ)=E(Sₙ) for every n.
Var(Sₙ)<Var(X̄ₙ) for all sufficiently large n.
X̄ₙ is consistent for μ.
X̄ₙ is sufficient for μ.

A.why: Both are weighted or unweighted linear combinations whose coefficients sum to one, so both have expectation μ.

B.why: Var(Sₙ)=1/Hₙ, where Hₙ=Σ(1/i), because Var(Xᵢ)=i. Since Hₙ→∞, this variance tends to zero, while Var(X̄ₙ)=(n+1)/(2n) tends to 1/2. Thus B is true.

C.why: Var(X̄ₙ)=(1/n²)Σi=(n+1)/(2n)→1/2, not zero, so X̄ₙ is not consistent.

D.why: With known unequal variances i, the likelihood depends on μ through the precision-weighted sum ΣXᵢ/i, not the ordinary sample mean alone.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 57 (December 2017), page 29. The supplied answer key on page 64 lists A and C, but direct calculation from the printed model (Var(Xᵢ)=i) gives A and B; this key discrepancy is explicitly retained for review. Since E(Xᵢ)=μ, both X̄ₙ and Sₙ=[Σ(Xᵢ/i)]/[Σ(1/i)] have expectation μ, so A is true. Let Hₙ=Σ(1/i). Independence and Var(Xᵢ)=i give Var(Sₙ)=Σ[(1/i)/Hₙ]²i=Hₙ/Hₙ²=1/Hₙ→0. Meanwhile Var(X̄ₙ)=Σi/n²=(n+1)/(2n)→1/2. Therefore B is true and X̄ₙ is not consistent, so C is false. The likelihood depends on μ through the precision-weighted sum ΣXᵢ/i, not the ordinary mean, so D is false. The mathematically supported combination is A and B only. Other-exam relevance: weighted estimation, consistency and sufficiency in heteroscedastic normal models overlap with UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. items.topic: inference-t4 · MLE consistency under a many-to-one sign transformation and bounded parameter space
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from N(θ,1), where −100≤θ≤100, and define Yᵢ=0 if Xᵢ<0 and Yᵢ=1 if Xᵢ≥0. Let θ̂ₙ and θ̃ₙ be the MLEs of θ based on the X-sample and Y-sample, respectively. Which statements are true?
statements: limₙ→∞ E(θ̂ₙ)=θ.
limₙ→∞ E(θ̃ₙ)=θ.
θ̂ₙ is a consistent estimator of θ.
θ̃ₙ is a consistent estimator of θ.

A.why: The full-sample MLE is the sample mean clipped to [−100,100]. Its expectation tends to θ as n grows.

B.why: Yᵢ is Bernoulli with success probability Φ(θ). The sign-based MLE is Φ⁻¹(Ȳ), clipped to the parameter interval at the endpoints; it converges to θ. Because it is bounded between −100 and 100, its expectation also converges to θ.

C.why: The sample mean converges in probability to θ by the law of large numbers, and the parameter constraint does not change this limit for θ in the interval.

D.why: Ȳ converges to Φ(θ), and the inverse normal cdf is continuous at Φ(θ) for finite θ, giving θ̃ₙ→θ in probability.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 58 (December 2017), page 30. The supplied answer key on page 64 lists all four statements, which agrees with the derivation. The full-sample MLE is X̄ₙ projected onto [−100,100]. Since X̄ₙ→θ and the parameter lies in this interval, the estimator is consistent; its expectation tends to θ, so A and C are true. For the sign-only sample, Yᵢ is Bernoulli with success probability Φ(θ). Its MLE is Φ⁻¹(Ȳₙ), clipped at the parameter endpoints when Ȳₙ is 0 or 1. Since Ȳₙ→Φ(θ), the estimator converges to θ, so D is true. It is bounded in [−100,100]; convergence in probability plus boundedness gives convergence of its expectation to θ, proving B. All four statements are true. items.topic: inference-t4 · maximum likelihood with right-censored exponential lifetime data and parameter constraints
items.stem: Twenty independent identical items have exponential lifetimes with mean θ, where 0<θ≤10. Testing begins at time 0 and stops when all 20 items have failed or at a fixed time T>0, whichever occurs first. Which statements about the MLE of θ are correct?
statements: The MLE of θ always exists.
The MLE of θ may not exist.
If it exists, the MLE is an unbiased estimator of θ.
If it exists, the MLE is bounded with probability one.

A.why: The parameter space is (0,10]. If no item fails before T, the likelihood increases up to the included endpoint θ=10. If r>0 failures are observed, the likelihood has a positive maximiser, truncated at 10 if needed.

B.why: The upper endpoint is included and the likelihood has a maximiser for both r=0 and r>0.

C.why: The censored-data MLE is a nonlinear, boundary-constrained function of the observed failure count and exposure time; it is not unbiased for all θ.

D.why: Every admissible MLE lies in the parameter space (0,10], so it is bounded by 10.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 59 (December 2017), page 30. The supplied answer key on page 64 lists A,D. Let r be the number of observed failures before the stopping time, and let E be the total time on test: the sum of the r observed failure times plus T for each of the 20−r survivors. For an exponential lifetime with mean θ, the likelihood, apart from factors not involving θ, is L(θ)∝θ^(−r)exp(−E/θ), with 0<θ≤10. If r>0, the log-likelihood is −r log θ−E/θ plus a constant. Differentiating gives −r/θ+E/θ²=0, so the unconstrained maximiser is E/r. Under the parameter restriction, the MLE is min(E/r,10). If r=0, L(θ)∝exp(−E/θ), which increases with θ, so the maximum occurs at θ=10. Therefore the MLE always exists: A true and B false. It always lies in (0,10], so D is true. It is not generally unbiased: censoring and the boundary truncation alter its sampling expectation, and an MLE is not automatically unbiased. Thus C is false. Correct answer: A and D only, option A. items.topic: regression-t2 · estimability, BLUE and unbiased residual variance estimation in the general linear model
items.stem: Consider the linear model Y=Xβ+ε, where X is an n×p design matrix, p<n, E(ε)=0 and Var(ε)=σ²I. Let β̂ solve the normal equations XᵀXβ̂=XᵀY. Which statements are true?
statements: If cᵀβ is estimable, then cᵀβ̂ is its BLUE.
All linear parametric functions are estimable if and only if rank(X)>p.
If rank(X)<p, then some linear parametric functions are not estimable.
(Y−Xβ̂)ᵀ(Y−Xβ̂)/(n−p) is always an unbiased estimator of σ².

A.why: The Gauss–Markov theorem applies to every estimable linear function; its least-squares estimator is the BLUE even when X is rank deficient.

B.why: For an n×p matrix, rank(X) cannot exceed p. All p-dimensional linear functions are estimable exactly when rank(X)=p, not when rank(X)>p.

C.why: If rank(X)<p, the row space of X is a proper subspace of Rᵖ, so at least one coefficient contrast is not estimable.

D.why: The residual sum of squares has expectation (n−rank(X))σ². Dividing by n−p is unbiased only when rank(X)=p.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 60 (June 2017), page 31. The supplied answer list ends at Q44. Let r=rank(X). In the general linear model, a linear function cᵀβ is estimable precisely when c lies in the row space of X. For any such c, the least-squares estimator cᵀβ̂ is unbiased and, by the Gauss–Markov theorem, has minimum variance among linear unbiased estimators. Thus A is true. Since X has p columns, rank(X)≤p; the condition printed in B, rank(X)>p, is impossible. The correct condition for every linear function of β to be estimable is full column rank, rank(X)=p. Thus B is false. If rank(X)<p, the row space is a proper subspace of Rᵖ, so some coefficient contrasts are not estimable; C is true. Finally, E(SSE)=(n−r)σ². Therefore SSE/(n−p) is unbiased only if r=p; the question does not assume full rank. D is false. The answer is A and C only, option A. Note: the scan explicitly prints “rank(X)>p” in statement B; it has not been silently corrected. Other-exam relevance: Gauss–Markov theory, estimability, rank conditions and residual variance estimation overlap with UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations. The supplied answer key on page 64 lists A, C and D. Statement D is unbiased if the usual full-column-rank condition rank(X)=p is assumed, because E(SSE)=(n−p)σ². The printed question only states p<n and does not explicitly state rank(X)=p; if rank(X)<p, E(SSE)=(n−rank(X))σ² and D is not unbiased. The bank therefore retains the literal-condition answer A and C, and flags the key's implicit full-rank assumption. Printed answer-key cross-check (source PDF page 64): Q60 is listed as A,C,D.

items.topic: inference-t4 · MLE when the parameter is restricted to the integers
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be independent N(θ,1) random variables, where θ is restricted to the integers {...,−2,−1,0,1,2,...}. What is the maximum-likelihood estimator of θ?
options: The largest integer not exceeding X̄
items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 61 (December 2016), page 32. No printed key is available in the supplied answer list. The likelihood is proportional to exp{−(1/2)Σ(Xᵢ−θ)²}. Use the identity Σ(Xᵢ−θ)²=Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²+n(X̄−θ)². The first term does not depend on θ, so maximising the likelihood is equivalent to choosing the allowed integer that minimises (X̄−θ)². That is the integer nearest to X̄. If X̄ is exactly halfway between two integers, both are maximisers; the phrase “integer closest” includes this tie. Therefore option B is correct. items.topic: inference-t4 · UMVU sample variance and maximum likelihood estimation of normal variance and standard deviation
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be an independent random sample from N(μ,σ²), where μ is unrestricted and σ²>0. Which statements are correct?
statements: S²=Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²/(n−1) is the minimum-variance unbiased estimator of σ².
The square root of S² is the minimum-variance unbiased estimator of σ.
Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²/n is the maximum-likelihood estimator of σ².
The square root of Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²/n is the maximum-likelihood estimator of σ.

A.why: For a normal sample, S² is unbiased for σ² and is a function of the complete sufficient statistic (ΣXᵢ,ΣXᵢ²), so it is UMVU.

B.why: The square root of an unbiased variance estimator is not generally unbiased for σ; Jensen's inequality gives E(√S²)<σ for a non-degenerate sample.

C.why: With μ unknown, maximising the normal likelihood gives μ̂=X̄ and σ̂²=Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²/n.

D.why: The MLE of σ is the square root of the MLE of σ², namely √[Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²/n].

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 62 (December 2016), page 32. The supplied answer list ends at Q44. For a normal sample with unknown mean and variance, the sample variance S²=Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²/(n−1) is unbiased for σ². The pair (ΣXᵢ,ΣXᵢ²) is complete and sufficient for (μ,σ²) in the full normal family, and S² is a function of it. By Lehmann–Scheffé, S² is the UMVU estimator of σ²; A is true. But taking a square root does not preserve unbiasedness. In fact, because the square-root function is concave, E(√S²)<√E(S²)=σ for a non-degenerate sample, so B is false. For maximum likelihood, the normal log-likelihood is maximised first at μ̂=X̄. Substituting this into the likelihood and differentiating with respect to σ² gives σ̂²_ML=Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²/n, not the n−1 version. Hence C is true, and the MLE of σ is its square root, making D true. Correct combination: A, C and D only, option B. items.topic: inference-t4 · sufficiency and unbiased estimation for a uniform location-scale family
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be independent Uniform(1−θ,1+θ) random variables, where θ>0. Write X_(1)=min(X₁,…,Xₙ), X_(n)=max(X₁,…,Xₙ), and X̄=(1/n)ΣXᵢ. Which statements are true?
statements: (X_(1), X̄, X_(n)) is sufficient for θ.
(X_(n)−X_(1))/2 is unbiased for θ.
(3/n)Σ(Xᵢ−1)² is unbiased for θ².
(3/n)Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)² is unbiased for θ².

A.why: The joint density is constant on the event X_(1)≥1−θ and X_(n)≤1+θ, so the likelihood depends on the sample through its minimum and maximum. Adding X̄ does not destroy sufficiency.

B.why: For this uniform distribution, E[X_(n)−X_(1)]=2θ(n−1)/(n+1), so half the range has expectation θ(n−1)/(n+1), not θ.

C.why: E[(X−1)²]=Var(X)=θ²/3. Therefore the expectation of (3/n)Σ(Xᵢ−1)² equals θ².

D.why: The expected centred sum of squares is (n−1)Var(X)=(n−1)θ²/3. Multiplying by 3/n gives (n−1)θ²/n, not θ².

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 63 (December 2016), page 33. No printed answer-key entry is available; the result is independently derived. The scan says “Which of the following is true?” but two statements are mathematically true, so the item is retained as multi-answer rather than forcing a single answer. The joint density is (2θ)^(−n) when every observation lies between 1−θ and 1+θ, and zero otherwise. The sample enters the likelihood through the smallest and largest observations, so (X_(1),X_(n)) is sufficient; any statistic that includes these two, such as (X_(1),X̄,X_(n)), is also sufficient. Thus A is true. For a sample from a uniform interval of width 2θ, E(X_(n)−X_(1))=2θ(n−1)/(n+1), so the half-range is biased downward; B is false. Also X−1 is Uniform(−θ,θ), so E[(X−1)²]=θ²/3. By linearity, E[(3/n)Σ(Xᵢ−1)²]=θ², proving C. Finally, E[Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²]=(n−1)Var(X)=(n−1)θ²/3; after multiplying by 3/n the expectation is (n−1)θ²/n, not θ². D is false. Hence A and C only are true, option A. items.topic: inference-t4 · MLE over a finite parameter space
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from N(θ,1), where θ∈{1,2}. Which statement about the maximum-likelihood estimator of θ is correct?
options: The MLE exists but is not X̄.
The MLE is an unbiased estimator of θ.
items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 64 (June 2016), page 33. The supplied answer key on page 64 lists C. The normal likelihood is proportional to exp{−(1/2)Σ(Xᵢ−θ)²}. Using Σ(Xᵢ−θ)²=Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²+n(X̄−θ)², choose whichever permitted value, 1 or 2, is closer to X̄. Equivalently, the MLE is 1 when X̄<1.5 and 2 when X̄>1.5; at X̄=1.5 both values maximise the likelihood. The estimator therefore exists, but it takes only the values 1 and 2 and is not the unrestricted sample mean. It is not generally unbiased either. Hence option C is correct. items.topic: regression-t2 · Gauss–Markov optimal linear unbiased estimation with correlated mean structure
items.stem: Let Y₁,Y₂,Y₃ be uncorrelated observations with common variance σ² and expectations E(Y₁)=β₁, E(Y₂)=β₂ and E(Y₃)=β₁+β₂. What is the BLUE of β₁+β₂?
items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 65 (June 2016), page 34. No printed answer-key entry is available; the result is independently derived. The supplied answer key on page 64 lists C. Consider a linear estimator aY₁+bY₂+cY₃. For it to be unbiased for β₁+β₂, its expectation aβ₁+bβ₂+c(β₁+β₂) must have coefficient 1 for both β₁ and β₂. Thus a+c=1 and b+c=1, so a=b=1−c. Since the observations are uncorrelated and have common variance σ², the estimator variance is σ²[a²+b²+c²]=σ²[2(1−c)²+c²]. Differentiate with respect to c: −4(1−c)+2c=0, giving c=2/3 and a=b=1/3. The BLUE is (Y₁+Y₂+2Y₃)/3, option C. This is a direct small Gauss–Markov optimisation: enforce unbiasedness first, then minimise the variance. Other-exam relevance: BLUE, linear unbiased estimation and variance minimisation overlap with UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. items.topic: inference-t4 · exponential lifetime likelihood and reliability of a series system
items.stem: A series system has two independent components. Each component lifetime has exponential density f(x)=λe^(−λx), x>0, with λ>0. Given n independent observed lifetimes X₁,…,Xₙ for one component and their mean X̄, what is the MLE of the system reliability at mission time t>0?
items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 66 (June 2016), page 34. The supplied answer key on page 64 lists C. For an exponential lifetime with rate λ, the reliability of one component at time t is R₁(t)=P(X>t)=e^(−λt). The two components are independent and are connected in series, so the system works only if both components survive beyond t. Therefore R_system(t)=R₁(t)²=e^(−2λt). For an exponential sample, the likelihood is proportional to λⁿexp(−λΣXᵢ), and differentiating its log gives λ̂=n/ΣXᵢ=1/X̄. Substitute this MLE into the system reliability: R̂_system(t)=exp(−2t/X̄). This is option C. items.topic: inference-t5 · method of moments and consistency for a shifted Gamma distribution
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from f(x;μ,α)=(1/Γ(α))(x−μ)^(α−1)e^(−(x−μ)), x≥μ, where −∞<μ<∞ and α>0. Which statements about method-of-moments estimators are correct?
statements: Method-of-moments estimators of both α and μ do not exist.
The method-of-moments estimator of α exists and is consistent.
The method-of-moments estimator of μ exists and is consistent.
Both method-of-moments estimators exist but are not consistent.

A.why: The first two moments provide two equations for the two unknown parameters, and they have a valid solution when the sample variance is positive.

B.why: The population variance is α, so the method-of-moments estimator is the sample second central moment (with denominator n), which converges to α by the law of large numbers.

C.why: The population mean is μ+α. Subtracting the variance parameter estimate from the sample mean gives μ̂_MOM=X̄−m₂, and this converges to μ.

D.why: Both estimators are functions of consistent sample moments, so both are consistent.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 67 (June 2016), page 35. The supplied answer list ends at Q44, so this is independently derived. The distribution is a Gamma(α, rate 1) variable shifted to the right by μ. For a Gamma variable with shape α and rate 1, the mean is α and variance is α. After shifting, E(X)=μ+α and Var(X)=α. The method-of-moments equations are therefore m₁=μ+α and m₂−m₁²=α, where m₁=X̄ and m₂=(1/n)ΣXᵢ² are the first two raw sample moments. Solving gives α̂_MOM=m₂−m₁² and μ̂_MOM=m₁−α̂_MOM. By the law of large numbers, m₁→E(X) and m₂→E(X²), so α̂_MOM→Var(X)=α and μ̂_MOM→E(X)−α=μ. Both estimators exist (apart from the degenerate zero-variance sample event) and are consistent. Thus B and C are true, option B. items.topic: inference-t7 · Bayesian estimation for a Poisson likelihood with an exponential prior
items.stem: Let X|λ have a Poisson distribution with parameter λ, and let λ have the exponential prior density f(λ)=e^(−λ), λ>0. Under squared-error loss, which statements are correct?
statements: The Bayes estimator of e^λ is 2^(X+1).
The posterior mean of λ is (X+1)/2.
The posterior distribution of λ is Gamma.
The Bayes estimator of e^(2λ) is 2^(2(X+1)).

A.why: The posterior is Gamma(shape X+1, rate 2). Its exponential moment at 1 is (2/(2−1))^(X+1)=2^(X+1).

B.why: The mean of a Gamma distribution with shape X+1 and rate 2 is (X+1)/2.

C.why: Multiplying the Poisson likelihood by the exponential prior gives a Gamma posterior kernel.

D.why: The posterior moment E[e^(2λ)|X] is infinite because the Gamma posterior rate is 2 and the requested exponential argument is also 2; the moment-generating function is finite only for t<2.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 68 (June 2016), page 35. The supplied answer key on page 64 lists A,B,C. Source-transcription caution: the low-resolution scan appears to show the prior support as z<0 in one line. That cannot define a probability density for e^(−z), because its integral over (−∞,0) diverges, and λ is a nonnegative Poisson rate. The bank therefore interprets the intended proper exponential prior as e^(−λ), λ>0; this correction is explicitly disclosed rather than attributed verbatim to the scan. The prior is exponential with rate 1, which is Gamma(shape 1, rate 1). The Poisson likelihood is proportional to λˣe^(−λ). Multiplying prior and likelihood gives the posterior kernel λˣe^(−2λ), so λ|X=x~Gamma(shape x+1, rate 2). Its posterior mean is (x+1)/2, proving B, and the posterior is Gamma, proving C. Under squared-error loss, the Bayes estimator of a function g(λ) is its posterior expectation. For a Gamma(k, rate r) variable, E(e^(tλ))=(r/(r−t))^k when t<r. With k=x+1 and r=2, E(e^λ|x)=(2/(2−1))^(x+1)=2^(x+1), so A is true. But E(e^(2λ)|x) is not finite: t=2 equals the posterior rate, and the integral diverges. Thus D is false. The correct combination is A, B and C only, option A. items.topic: inference-t4 · consistency, efficiency and sufficiency for a uniform location model
items.stem: Let X₁,…,X₂ₙ₊₁ be a random sample from Uniform(θ−1,θ+1). Let T₁=X̄, T₂ be the sample median and T₃=(T₁+T₂)/2. Which statements are correct?
statements: T₁ is consistent for θ.
Both T₁ and T₂ are more efficient than T₃.
All three estimators are unbiased for θ.
T₂ is sufficient for θ.

A.why: The sample mean converges to E(X)=θ by the law of large numbers.

B.why: The sample mean is more efficient than T₃, but the median is less efficient than T₃; averaging the mean and median reduces the median's variance.

C.why: Symmetry about θ makes both the sample mean and the odd-sample median unbiased; their average is unbiased too.

D.why: For a uniform location model with known width, the likelihood depends on the sample minimum and maximum, not the median alone.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 70 (June 2016), page 37. The supplied answer key on page 64 lists A,C. Symmetry gives E(T₁)=E(T₂)=θ, so T₃ is unbiased too; C is true. The sample mean is consistent by the law of large numbers, so A is true. Put m=2n+1. For Uniform(θ−1,θ+1), Var(T₁)=1/(3m), Var(T₂)=1/(m+2), and Cov(T₁,T₂)=(m+1)/[2m(m+2)]. Thus Var(T₃)=(7m+5)/[12m(m+2)], which lies between Var(T₁) and Var(T₂): the mean is more efficient than T₃, but the median is not. B is false. The likelihood depends on the sample extremes, so the median alone is not sufficient; D is false. Answer A and C only. items.topic: inference-t4 · MLE for a uniform scale family with parameter-dependent support
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from Uniform(θ,5θ), θ>0. Let X_(1) and X_(n) be the sample minimum and maximum. What is the MLE of θ?
items.explanation: For a sample from Uniform(θ,5θ), the likelihood is L(θ)=θ⁻ⁿ when every observation lies in the interval. The support constraints are θ≤X₍₁₎ and X₍ₙ₎≤5θ, so X₍ₙ₎/5≤θ≤X₍₁₎. Since θ⁻ⁿ decreases as θ increases, the likelihood is maximised at the smallest admissible value, θ̂=X₍ₙ₎/5, option D. This is a boundary MLE arising from parameter-dependent support. items.topic: inference-t4 · unbiased variance estimation from independent linear contrasts
items.stem: Let Y₁,Y₂,Y₃,Y₄ be uncorrelated with common variance σ² and E(Y₁)=E(Y₂), E(Y₃)=E(Y₄). Define e₁=(Y₁−Y₂)/√2 and e₂=(Y₃−Y₄)/√2. Which expression is unbiased for σ²?
items.explanation: Because Y₁ and Y₂ are uncorrelated and have equal means, E(e₁)=0. Also Var(e₁)=[Var(Y₁)+Var(Y₂)]/2=σ², so E(e₁²)=σ². The same argument gives E(e₂²)=σ². Therefore E[(e₁²+e₂²)/2]=(σ²+σ²)/2=σ², making option B unbiased. The other options have expectations 0, σ²/2 or 2σ², respectively. items.topic: inference-t4 · MLE from triangular parameter-dependent support
items.stem: A random sample of size n is drawn uniformly from the triangle with vertices (0,0), (0,θ) and (θ,0), θ>0. What is the MLE of θ?
items.explanation: The joint density of each observation is 2/θ² on the triangular support x≥0, y≥0, x+y≤θ. For a sample of n pairs, the likelihood is (2/θ²)ⁿ provided θ≥maxᵢ(Xᵢ+Yᵢ), and zero otherwise. Within the allowed parameter set this likelihood decreases as θ increases. Its maximum is therefore attained at the smallest allowed value, θ̂=maxᵢ(Xᵢ+Yᵢ), option C. Source: supplied Estimation CSIR NET scan, printed Question 73 (December 2015). items.topic: inference-t3 · Poisson factorial moments and Lehmann–Scheffé UMVU estimation
items.stem: Let X~Poisson(λ), λ>0. To estimate λ⁵, consider T=X(X−1)(X−2)(X−3)(X−4). Which statement is true?
options: T is unbiased but not UMVU.
A UMVU estimator does not exist.
items.explanation: For a Poisson random variable, the fifth falling-factorial moment is E[X(X−1)(X−2)(X−3)(X−4)]=λ⁵. Thus T is unbiased for λ⁵. The statistic X is sufficient and complete for λ in the Poisson family; T is a function of X. By the Lehmann–Scheffé theorem, this unbiased function of a complete sufficient statistic is the UMVU estimator. Hence option C. items.topic: inference-t4 · likelihood and unbiased estimation for a geometric distribution
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid geometric with P(Xᵢ=k)=p(1−p)^(k−1), k=1,2,…, and let f count observations equal to 1. Which statements are true?
statements: f/n is the MLE of p.
f/n is unbiased for p.
(n−1)/ΣXᵢ is the MLE of p.
Var(f/n)=p(1−p)/n.

A.why: The likelihood gives p̂=n/ΣXᵢ, not f/n.

B.why: P(Xᵢ=1)=p under the one-based geometric convention, so f is Binomial(n,p).

C.why: Differentiating the likelihood gives n/ΣXᵢ; the numerator is n, not n−1.

D.why: Since f~Binomial(n,p), Var(f/n)=p(1−p)/n.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 83 (June 2014), page 44. The supplied answer key on page 64 lists B,D. The scan omits the support convention, so this entry explicitly uses the one-based geometric law P(X=k)=p(1−p)^(k−1), k≥1. Then Iᵢ=1{Xᵢ=1} is Bernoulli(p), and f=ΣIᵢ~Binomial(n,p). Thus E(f/n)=p and Var(f/n)=p(1−p)/n: B and D are true. The sample likelihood is pⁿ(1−p)^(ΣXᵢ−n). Differentiating its log gives n/p−(ΣXᵢ−n)/(1−p)=0, so p̂=n/ΣXᵢ. Hence A and C are false. If a zero-based geometric convention were intended, the answer would differ; the scan does not specify this, so the convention is disclosed. items.stem: A discrete model has parameter pair (θ₁,θ₂) in {(1/3,3),(1/2,2),(2,1/2),(3,1/3)}. If X=3 is observed, which parameter pair is the MLE?

items.topic: inference-t2 · sufficiency, completeness and ancillary ratios in a uniform scale family
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid Uniform(θ,3θ), θ>0, with minimum X_(1) and maximum X_(n). Which statements are true?
statements: (X_(n)−X_(1))/2 is unbiased for θ.
(X_(1),X_(n)) is complete sufficient for θ.
X_(n)/(X_(1)+X_(n)) is ancillary.
(1/(2n))ΣXᵢ is unbiased for θ.

A.why: The expected range is 2θ(n−1)/(n+1), so half the range is biased.

B.why: The extremes are sufficient, but their non-degenerate scale-free ratio is ancillary, so the pair is not complete.

C.why: The ratio is unchanged by scaling all observations by θ, so its distribution does not depend on θ.

D.why: E(Xᵢ)=2θ, so the average divided by 2 is unbiased for θ.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 86 (December 2013), page 47. The supplied answer key on page 64 lists C,D. The joint likelihood depends on the observations through their minimum and maximum, so the pair is sufficient. But X_(n)/(X_(1)+X_(n)) is unchanged when every observation is divided by θ; its distribution is therefore parameter-free and it is ancillary. Since it is a non-constant function of the sufficient pair, that pair is not complete, so B is false. For Uniform(θ,3θ), E(Xᵢ)=2θ, making (1/(2n))ΣXᵢ unbiased; D is true. Also E(X_(n)−X_(1))=2θ(n−1)/(n+1), so half the range is biased and A is false. C and D only are true, option C. items.topic: inference-t4 · consistent estimation from rounded exponential observations
items.stem: Let X be exponential with mean 1/θ, θ>0, but only Y=floor(X) is observed, where Y=k if k≤X<k+1. For iid Y₁,…,Yₙ, which is a consistent estimator of θ?
items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 87 (December 2013), page 47. The supplied answer key on page 64 lists B and C. Since X is exponential with rate θ, P(Y=k)=e^(−θk)−e^(−θ(k+1))=(1−e^(−θ))e^(−θk), k=0,1,… . This geometric distribution has mean E(Y)=1/(e^θ−1). By the law of large numbers, Ȳ→1/(e^θ−1), so ln(1+1/Ȳ)=ln(1+n/ΣYᵢ) converges to θ. The estimator ln(1+(n+1)/ΣYᵢ) has the same limit because (n+1)/ΣYᵢ=((n+1)/n)(1/Ȳ) and (n+1)/n→1. Thus B and C are both consistent, as the key states. A and D converge to e^θ−1, not θ. ln(1+n/ΣYᵢ)

A.why: n/ΣYᵢ=1/Ȳ does not converge to θ; it converges to e^θ−1.

items.topic: inference-t1 · conditional distributions and sufficiency in the exponential family
items.stem: Let X₁ and X₂ be independent exponential random variables with common mean θ>0. Given X₁+X₂=t, what is the conditional distribution of X₂?

items.stem: Consider Yᵢ=a+(−1)ⁱb+εᵢ, i=1,…,n, n≥3, where εᵢ are independent N(0,σ²). Which statement is correct?
options: The MLEs of a and b always exist.
The MLEs of a and b always exist, but may not be unique.
The MLE of σ² does not exist.
The MLEs of a and b are not consistent.
items.explanation: The conditional mean is a+(−1)ⁱb. The design matrix has two columns: a column of ones and a column alternating between −1 and +1. For n≥3, both signs occur, so these columns are linearly independent and the design matrix has rank 2. The normal linear model therefore has a unique least-squares estimate, which is also the MLE of (a,b). Thus option A is correct. items.topic: inference-t4 · unbiased and consistent estimation for a Gamma rate parameter
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid with density f(x)=(1/2)λ³x²e^(−λx), x>0, λ>0. Which statements are true?
statements: (2/n)Σ(1/Xᵢ) is unbiased for λ.
3n/ΣXᵢ is unbiased for λ.
(2/n)Σ(1/Xᵢ) is consistent for λ.
3n/ΣXᵢ is consistent for λ.

A.why: X is Gamma(shape 3, rate λ), so E(1/X)=λ/(3−1)=λ/2.

B.why: The sum is Gamma(shape 3n, rate λ), so E[3n/ΣXᵢ]=3nλ/(3n−1), not λ.

C.why: The variables 1/Xᵢ have finite mean λ/2, so the law of large numbers gives convergence of their average to λ/2.

D.why: X̄ converges to E(X)=3/λ, so 3/X̄=3n/ΣXᵢ converges to λ.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 90 (June 2013), page 50. The supplied answer key on page 65 lists A,C,D. The density is Gamma with shape 3 and rate λ. For a Gamma(shape α, rate λ) variable, E(1/X)=λ/(α−1) when α>1. Here α=3, so E(1/X)=λ/2. Therefore (2/n)Σ(1/Xᵢ) is unbiased for λ, proving A. The sum S=ΣXᵢ is Gamma(shape 3n, rate λ), and E(1/S)=λ/(3n−1). Thus E(3n/S)=3nλ/(3n−1), not λ; B is false. Since E(1/Xᵢ)=λ/2 is finite, the law of large numbers makes (2/n)Σ(1/Xᵢ) converge to λ, so C is true. Also X̄→E(X)=3/λ, so 3/X̄=3n/ΣXᵢ→λ, proving D. Correct combination A, C and D only, option B. items.topic: inference-t4 · non-unique MLEs for a uniform location model
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid Uniform(θ−2,θ+2), with sample minimum X_(1) and maximum X_(n). Which of the following are maximum-likelihood estimators of θ?

A.why: The lower feasible endpoint for θ is X_(n)−2, not X_(1)−2.

B.why: The upper feasible endpoint is X_(1)+2, not X_(n)+2.

C.why: The MLE set is [X_(n)−2, X_(1)+2]. The midpoint of the sample extremes lies in this interval whenever the sample range is at most 4.

D.why: This is a convex combination of the two endpoints X_(1)+2 and X_(n)−2, so it also lies in the MLE interval.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 91 (June 2013), page 51. The supplied answer key on page 65 lists C,D. The likelihood is constant in θ whenever every observation lies in (θ−2,θ+2), and zero otherwise. The support restrictions give θ≤X_(1)+2 and θ≥X_(n)−2. Therefore every θ in [X_(n)−2, X_(1)+2] maximises the likelihood; the MLE is not unique. The midpoint (X_(1)+X_(n))/2 lies in this interval, so C is an MLE. D is a convex combination of the interval endpoints X_(1)+2 and X_(n)−2, so it is also an MLE. A and B are not the feasible endpoints and are not generally MLEs. Thus C and D only are correct, option C. items.stem: A circle's radius is measured with independent normal errors of mean zero and variance σ². Let X̄ and s² be the sample mean and unbiased sample variance of n radius measurements. Which expression is an unbiased estimator of the circle's area πR²?

Option D subtracts σ² rather than σ²/n from X̄², so it is not unbiased in general. items.topic: inference-t2 · sufficiency, ancillary statistics and consistency for a uniform location family
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid Uniform(θ−5,θ−3), with sample minimum X_(1) and maximum X_(n). Which statements are always true?
statements: (X_(1),X_(n)) is complete sufficient for θ.
X₁+X₂−2X₃ is ancillary.
X_(n)+3 is unbiased for θ.
X_(1)+5 is consistent for θ.

A.why: The extremes are sufficient, but a non-degenerate parameter-free function of them prevents completeness.

B.why: The coefficients 1+1−2 sum to zero, so the location parameter cancels and the distribution does not depend on θ.

C.why: E(X_(n))=θ−3−2/(n+1), so adding 3 leaves a downward bias.

D.why: The sample minimum converges to the lower endpoint θ−5 as n grows, so X_(1)+5 converges to θ.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 93 (December 2012), page 52. The supplied answer key on page 65 lists B,D. The sample extremes are sufficient because the likelihood depends on the sample through the minimum and maximum. However, the pair is not complete: X₁+X₂−2X₃ has coefficients summing to zero, so the location parameter θ cancels and its distribution is parameter-free. This is a non-degenerate ancillary statistic, making A false and B true. The expected sample maximum from Uniform(θ−5,θ−3) is θ−3−2/(n+1), so X_(n)+3 is biased downward; C is false. The sample minimum converges to the lower endpoint θ−5, so X_(1)+5 is consistent for θ; D is true. Correct combination B and D only, option B. items.topic: inference-t7 · Bayesian estimation with an exponential prior and Poisson likelihood
items.stem: Let X~Poisson(θ), and suppose the prior distribution of θ is exponential with median ln 2. Under squared-error loss, which statements are necessarily true?
statements: The posterior distribution is Gamma.
The prior is conjugate.
The posterior mean is (x+1)ln 2/(1+ln 2).
The Bayes estimator of θ is (x+1)/2.

A.why: An exponential prior is Gamma(shape 1); multiplying by a Poisson likelihood gives a Gamma posterior.

B.why: The Gamma family is conjugate to the Poisson likelihood.

C.why: An exponential distribution with median ln 2 has rate 1, not rate 1/ln 2. The posterior mean is (x+1)/2.

D.why: The posterior is Gamma(shape x+1, rate 2), whose mean is (x+1)/2.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 94 (December 2012), page 52. The supplied answer key on page 65 lists A,B,D. For an exponential distribution with rate r, the median is ln(2)/r. A prior median of ln 2 therefore means r=1. The prior is Gamma(shape 1, rate 1). The Poisson likelihood is proportional to θˣe^(−θ), so multiplying prior and likelihood gives posterior density proportional to θˣe^(−2θ), a Gamma(shape x+1, rate 2) distribution. Thus A and B are true. Its posterior mean is (x+1)/2, which is the Bayes estimator under squared-error loss, proving D. Statement C uses the wrong rate interpretation and is false. The correct combination is A, B and D only, option B. items.topic: inference-t4 · comparison of MLE and UMVU variance estimators by mean squared error
items.stem: For a normal sample of size n≥2 with unknown mean and variance σ², let σ̂²_MLE and σ̂²_UMVU denote the maximum-likelihood and UMVU estimators of σ². Which statement is correct?
options: The MLE has larger variance than the UMVU estimator.
The MLE has smaller mean squared error than the UMVU estimator.
They have the same mean squared error.
items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 95 (June 2012), page 53. The supplied answer key on page 65 lists C. Let S²=Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²/(n−1), the unbiased UMVU estimator. The normal MLE is σ̂²_MLE=(n−1)S²/n. Since Var(S²)=2σ⁴/(n−1), Var(σ̂²_MLE)=2(n−1)σ⁴/n², which is smaller than Var(S²)=2σ⁴/(n−1). The MLE is biased downward by −σ²/n. Its mean squared error is variance plus squared bias: MSE(σ̂²_MLE)=[2(n−1)+1]σ⁴/n²=(2n−1)σ⁴/n². The UMVU estimator is unbiased, so its MSE is its variance, 2σ⁴/(n−1). The MLE's MSE is smaller for n≥2. Therefore option C is correct. The UMVU estimator minimises variance among unbiased estimators; it does not necessarily minimise MSE among biased estimators. Other-exam relevance: MLE, UMVU and bias–variance trade-offs overlap with UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. items.topic: inference-t1 · complete sufficient statistics for independent exponential observations with different rates
items.stem: Let X₁ and X₂ be independent with densities f₁(x)=θ⁻¹e^(−x/θ) and f₂(x)=2θ⁻¹e^(−2x/θ), x>0. Which statements are true?
statements: X₁+X₂ is sufficient for θ.
X₁+2X₂ is sufficient for θ.
X₁+2X₂ is complete for θ.
(X₁+2X₂)/2 is unbiased for θ.

A.why: The joint likelihood depends on θ through X₁+2X₂, not X₁+X₂.

B.why: The joint density factors into a θ-free term times a function of θ and X₁+2X₂.

C.why: X₁ and 2X₂ are independent exponential variables with common mean θ; their sum is Gamma(shape 2, scale θ), a complete one-parameter scale-family statistic.

D.why: E(X₁)=θ and E(2X₂)=θ, so the half-sum has expectation θ.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 97 (June 2012), page 54. The supplied answer key on page 65 lists B,C,D. The joint density is proportional to θ^(−2)exp[−(X₁+2X₂)/θ]. Thus the likelihood depends on the sample through X₁+2X₂, making B true and A false. Also X₁ is exponential with mean θ, and 2X₂ is exponential with mean θ. They are independent, so their sum has a Gamma distribution with shape 2 and scale θ. This is a complete sufficient statistic for θ, proving C. Since E(X₁)=θ and E(2X₂)=θ, E[(X₁+2X₂)/2]=θ, so D is true. Correct combination B, C and D only, option C. items.topic: inference-t4 · MSE comparison of biased and unbiased normal variance estimators
items.stem: For an iid normal sample of size n≥2 with unknown mean and variance σ², which statements are true?
statements: The MLE of σ² is unbiased.
The UMVU estimator of σ² has smaller MSE than the MLE.
Both the MLE and UMVU estimator are consistent.
For every unbiased estimator of σ², there is another estimator with smaller MSE.

A.why: The MLE divides the residual sum of squares by n, so its expectation is (n−1)σ²/n.

B.why: For the normal model, the biased MLE has smaller MSE than the unbiased sample variance.

C.why: Both estimators converge in probability to σ² as n grows.

D.why: The MLE has lower MSE than the UMVU estimator; every unbiased estimator has variance at least that of the UMVU estimator, so the MLE also has smaller MSE than any unbiased estimator.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 98 (June 2012), page 54. The supplied answer key on page 65 lists C,D. The MLE is Sₙ²=Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²/n. Since E[Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²]=(n−1)σ², its expectation is (n−1)σ²/n, so it is biased; A is false. The UMVU estimator is S²=Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²/(n−1). Its variance and MSE are 2σ⁴/(n−1). The MLE has MSE (2n−1)σ⁴/n², which is smaller for n≥2; B is false. Both are constant multiples of the same residual sum of squares and converge to σ², so C is true. The UMVU property gives Var(U)≥Var(S²) for every unbiased estimator U. Since the MLE's MSE is smaller than Var(S²), it is smaller than the MSE of every unbiased estimator. Thus D is true. Correct combination C and D only, option C. Other-exam relevance: MLE, UMVU, consistency and MSE comparisons overlap with UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. items.topic: inference-t4 · unbiasedness and UMVU estimation in a uniform location model
items.stem: Let X₁,…,X₂₅ be iid Uniform(θ−1/2,θ+1/2), where θ is unknown. Which statements are true?
statements: The sample mean is unbiased for θ.
The sample median is unbiased for θ.
The sample mean is not the UMVU estimator of θ.
The sample median is not the UMVU estimator of θ.

A.why: The uniform distribution is symmetric about θ, so E(X̄)=θ.

B.why: For an odd sample from a distribution symmetric about θ, the sample median is unbiased for θ.

C.why: Conditioning the sample mean on the sufficient pair (minimum, maximum) gives their midpoint, which has smaller variance than the sample mean.

D.why: The same conditional expectation argument reduces the variance of the sample median; it is not UMVU either.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 99 (June 2012), page 55. The supplied answer key on page 65 lists A,B,C,D. The distribution is symmetric about θ, so both the sample mean and the sample median are unbiased; A and B are true. For a uniform distribution with known interval width, the sufficient statistic is the pair (X_(1),X_(n)). Given these extremes, the remaining n−2 observations are distributed uniformly between them. The conditional expectation of the sample mean given the extremes is (X_(1)+X_(n))/2. This Rao–Blackwellised estimator is unbiased and has no larger variance, and in this non-degenerate case it has strictly smaller variance. Therefore the sample mean is not UMVU, so C is true. Conditioning the sample median on the same sufficient statistic also gives the midpoint by symmetry of the interior order statistics; its variance is reduced as well. Thus the median is not UMVU either, so D is true. All four statements are true, option D. items.topic: inference-t5 · method of moments for an exponential distribution observed after discretisation
items.stem: Let X have exponential density f(x;λ)=λe^(−λx), x>0. The observed variable is Y=k when k<X≤k+1, k=0,1,2,… . For a sample Y₁,…,Yₙ with mean Ȳ, which statements are true about the method-of-moments estimator of λ?
statements: The method-of-moments estimator is the same as the maximum-likelihood estimator.

A.why: The mean of the discretised geometric variable is not 1/λ.

B.why: Adding one to 1/Ȳ does not solve the moment equation.

C.why: The discretised variable has mean 1/(e^λ−1), so solving Ȳ=1/(e^λ−1) gives λ̂=ln(1+1/Ȳ).

D.why: The likelihood of the geometric observations has the same maximiser, ln(1+n/ΣYᵢ)=ln(1+1/Ȳ).

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 100 (June 2012), page 55. The supplied answer key on page 65 lists C,D. For Y=k when k<X≤k+1, P(Y=k)=e^(−λk)−e^(−λ(k+1))=(1−e^(−λ))e^(−λk), k=0,1,… . This is a geometric distribution on the nonnegative integers with mean E(Y)=e^(−λ)/(1−e^(−λ))=1/(e^λ−1). The method-of-moments equation is Ȳ=1/(e^λ−1). Rearranging gives e^λ=1+1/Ȳ and λ̂=ln(1+1/Ȳ), so C is true. The likelihood is proportional to (1−e^(−λ))ⁿe^(−λΣYᵢ); differentiating its log gives the same estimate ln(1+n/ΣYᵢ)=ln(1+1/Ȳ). Thus D is true, while A and B are false. Correct combination C and D only, option C. Other-exam relevance: method of moments, geometric distributions and likelihood for discretised data overlap with UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. items.topic: inference-t4 · unbiasedness and consistency of sample variance and standard deviation
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid with finite mean μ and variance σ². Define Sₙ=√{Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²/(n−1)}. Which statements are true?
statements: Sₙ is unbiased for σ.
Sₙ² is unbiased for σ².
Sₙ is consistent for σ.
Sₙ² is consistent for σ².

A.why: The square root of an unbiased variance estimator is generally biased downward; E(Sₙ) is not σ in general.

B.why: The sample variance with denominator n−1 is unbiased for the population variance σ².

C.why: The sample variance converges to σ², and continuity of the square root gives Sₙ→σ.

D.why: The sample variance is consistent for σ² under the stated finite-variance iid assumptions.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 102 (December 2011), page 56. The supplied answer-key sheet (PDF page 65) lists A and B. That key does not agree with the stated definition: Sₙ² is the unbiased sample variance, while Sₙ is generally biased; both are consistent under the stated iid finite-variance assumptions. The mathematically supported answer is therefore B, C and D only. This is a source-key discrepancy, not a silent correction. By definition, Sₙ²=Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²/(n−1) is the usual sample variance, and its expectation is σ². Thus B is true. Taking a square root does not preserve unbiasedness: because the square-root function is concave, E(Sₙ)≤√E(Sₙ²)=σ, with strict inequality in non-degenerate cases. Thus A is false. Under iid sampling with finite variance, the sample variance converges in probability to σ². Applying the continuous mapping theorem to the square root gives Sₙ→σ, so C and D are true. Correct combination B, C and D only, option B. Under the stated general iid finite-variance assumptions, Sₙ is not generally unbiased for σ, while Sₙ² is unbiased for σ² and both are consistent. items.topic: inference-t3 · UMVU estimation of a normal variance when the mean is known
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid N(0,σ²), where σ² is unknown. What is the minimum-variance unbiased estimator of σ²?

items.topic: inference-t1 · factorisation and sufficiency for independent uniforms with shifted supports
items.stem: Suppose X₁~Uniform(0,θ) and X₂~Uniform(0,1+θ) independently, where θ>0. Which statistic is sufficient for θ?
items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 106 (June 2011), page 58. The supplied answer key on page 65 lists —. The joint density is 1/[θ(1+θ)] when 0<X₁<θ and 0<X₂<1+θ, and zero otherwise. These support conditions can be rewritten as θ>X₁ and θ>X₂−1, or θ>max(X₁,X₂−1). The likelihood therefore depends on the sample through max(X₁,X₂−1), apart from a factor involving θ only. By the factorisation theorem, this maximum is sufficient. Option C is correct. items.topic: inference-t4 · constrained normal MLE, UMVU estimation and risk comparison
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid N(μ,1), where μ≥0 is unknown. Which statements are true?
statements: The MLE and UMVU estimator of μ are the same.
The UMVU estimator of μ is consistent.
For every unbiased estimator of μ, there is another estimator with smaller MSE.
The MLE has smaller MSE than the method-of-moments estimator.

A.why: The MLE is max(X̄,0), while X̄ is unbiased and UMVU; the constrained MLE is generally biased.

B.why: The UMVU estimator is X̄, which converges to μ by the law of large numbers.

C.why: The positive-part estimator max(X̄,0) has lower MSE than the unbiased X̄ for μ≥0, and X̄ has minimum variance among unbiased estimators.

D.why: The method-of-moments estimator is X̄. The constrained positive-part MLE reduces squared error by replacing negative sample means with zero when μ≥0.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 107 (June 2011), page 58. The supplied answer key on page 65 lists —. The likelihood is maximised by projecting the unrestricted sample mean onto the allowed parameter space μ≥0, so μ̂_MLE=max(X̄,0). The normal family has complete sufficient statistic X̄, and X̄ is unbiased for μ; therefore X̄ is the UMVU estimator. It is consistent, so B is true. Since the MLE differs from X̄ whenever X̄<0, A is false. The positive-part estimator cannot increase squared error when the true μ is nonnegative: if X̄<0, replacing X̄ by zero is closer to μ; otherwise it leaves X̄ unchanged. Thus its MSE is smaller than that of X̄. As every unbiased estimator has variance at least that of the UMVU estimator X̄, C follows. The method-of-moments estimator is X̄, so D is true as well. Correct combination B, C and D only, option B. items.topic: inference-t7 · Gamma–Poisson conjugacy and posterior mean
items.stem: For a Poisson mean λ, use a Gamma prior with density proportional to e^(−βλ)λ^(α−1), α,β>0. Given a sample of size n with sample mean X̄, which statements about the posterior are true?
statements: The posterior distribution is Gamma.
The posterior distribution is Poisson.
The posterior mean is (nX̄+α)/(n+β).
The posterior mean is (nX̄+α)(n+β).

A.why: Multiplying the Gamma prior kernel by the Poisson likelihood gives a Gamma posterior kernel.

B.why: The parameter λ is continuous; the posterior is Gamma, not Poisson.

C.why: The posterior shape is nX̄+α and its rate is n+β, so its mean is their ratio.

D.why: A Gamma mean is shape divided by rate, not their product.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 109 (June 2011), page 59. The supplied answer key on page 65 lists —. The Poisson likelihood for a sample is proportional to λ^(ΣXᵢ)e^(−nλ). The prior kernel is λ^(α−1)e^(−βλ). Multiplying gives λ^(ΣXᵢ+α−1)e^(−(n+β)λ), which is the kernel of a Gamma distribution with shape α+ΣXᵢ=α+nX̄ and rate β+n. Thus A is true and B false. A Gamma(shape a, rate b) variable has mean a/b, so the posterior mean is (nX̄+α)/(n+β), proving C; D is false. items.topic: inference-t3 · UMVU estimation and Cramér–Rao bounds for an exponential rate
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid exponential with density f(x;θ)=θe^(−θx), x>0, θ>0, and let Tₙ=X̄. Which statements are true?
statements: The UMVU estimator of θ is (n−1)/(nTₙ).
The Cramér–Rao lower bound for the variance of any unbiased estimator of θ is θ²/n.
The UMVU estimator attains the Cramér–Rao lower bound.
1−e^(−1/Tₙ) is a consistent estimator of Pθ(X₁≤1).

A.why: The sum of exponential observations is complete sufficient and the inverse-sum estimator (n−1)/ΣXᵢ is unbiased for θ.

B.why: The Fisher information in n exponential observations is n/θ², so the CRLB is θ²/n.

C.why: The variance of the UMVU estimator is θ²/(n−2) for n>2, which exceeds θ²/n.

D.why: Tₙ converges to 1/θ, so 1−exp(−1/Tₙ) converges to 1−e^(−θ)=Pθ(X≤1).

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 111 (June 2024), page 60. The supplied answer-key sheet (PDF page 65) lists statements 1, 2 and 4, matching option B. The sample sum S=ΣXᵢ is Gamma(shape n, rate θ), and it is complete sufficient for θ. Since E(1/S)=θ/(n−1), the estimator (n−1)/S=(n−1)/(nTₙ) is unbiased and, by Lehmann–Scheffé, UMVU; A is true. The Fisher information from one exponential observation is 1/θ², so for n observations it is n/θ². The Cramér–Rao bound is θ²/n, proving B. The UMVU estimator's variance is θ²/(n−2) for n>2, which is not equal to θ²/n, so it does not attain the bound; C is false. Finally Tₙ→1/θ, and the continuous mapping theorem gives 1−e^(−1/Tₙ)→1−e^(−θ)=Pθ(X₁≤1). Thus D is true. items.topic: inference-t1 · inference-t2 · minimal sufficiency, completeness and ancillary statistics for Bernoulli samples
items.stem: Let X,Y,Z be iid Bernoulli(θ), 0<θ<1. Which statements are true?
statements: (79X+202Y, 23Z²) is sufficient for θ.
13(X+Y+Z)³ is minimal sufficient for θ.
2(X+Y+Z) is complete sufficient for θ.
X−2Y+Z is ancillary.

A.why: Since Z²=Z and the two weighted components identify X, Y and Z, the statistic encodes the full sample and is sufficient.

B.why: The sum S=X+Y+Z is minimal sufficient for the Bernoulli parameter; the map 13S³ is one-to-one on S∈{0,1,2,3}.

C.why: S~Binomial(3,θ), a complete sufficient statistic for θ; multiplying by 2 does not change completeness or sufficiency.

D.why: The distribution of X−2Y+Z depends on θ, so it is not ancillary.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 113 (December 2024), page 61. The supplied answer-key sheet (PDF page 65) lists statements 1, 2 and 3, matching option B. For three iid Bernoulli observations, the likelihood is proportional to θ^S(1−θ)^(3−S), where S=X+Y+Z. Hence S is minimal sufficient. Since S has a Binomial(3,θ) distribution, it is complete as well. Any one-to-one function of S on its possible values {0,1,2,3}, including 13S³ and 2S, remains minimal sufficient or complete sufficient respectively. Statement C is true. The pair in A also identifies the full sample: 23Z²=23Z reveals Z, and 79X+202Y uniquely distinguishes the four possibilities for (X,Y). A is true. By contrast, X−2Y+Z has a distribution that varies with θ; for example, its probability of being zero is not constant in θ. D is false. Therefore A, B and C are true, option B. Other-exam relevance: Bernoulli sufficiency, completeness and ancillary statistics overlap with UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. items.topic: inference-t3 · complete sufficient statistics and UMVU estimators for a uniform location-scale family
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ, n≥3, be iid Uniform(θ₁−θ₂,θ₁+θ₂), where θ₁∈R and θ₂>0. Assume (X_(1),X_(n)) is complete sufficient for (θ₁,θ₂). Which statements are true?
statements: X̄ is unbiased for θ₁.
X̄−X_(1) is unbiased for θ₂.
(X_(1)+X_(n))/2 is the UMVU estimator of θ₁.
(n+1)(X_(n)−X_(1))/[2(n−1)] is the UMVU estimator of θ₂.

A.why: The interval is symmetric about θ₁, so E(X̄)=θ₁.

C.why: The midpoint of the extremes is unbiased for θ₁ and is a function of the complete sufficient pair, so it is UMVU.

D.why: The range has expectation 2θ₂(n−1)/(n+1); the displayed scaling makes it unbiased and it is a function of the complete sufficient pair.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 116 (June 2025), page 62. The supplied answer-key sheet (PDF page 65) lists statements 1, 3 and 4, matching option B. The distribution is centred at θ₁, so E(X̄)=θ₁ and A is true. For a sample from an interval of width 2θ₂, E(X_(1))=θ₁−θ₂+2θ₂/(n+1). Therefore E(X̄−X_(1))=θ₂−2θ₂/(n+1)=θ₂(n−1)/(n+1), so B is false. The midpoint of the sample extremes has expectation θ₁ and is a function of the assumed complete sufficient statistic; by Lehmann–Scheffé it is UMVU for θ₁. The expected range is 2θ₂(n−1)/(n+1), so multiplying the range by (n+1)/[2(n−1)] gives an unbiased estimator of θ₂. It too is a function of the complete sufficient pair and is UMVU. Thus A, C and D are true, option B. items.topic: inference-t4 · method-of-moments consistency for a Laplace location-scale model
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ, n≥2, be iid with Laplace density f(x|θ)=(1/(2θ))exp(−|x−θ|/θ), x∈R, θ>0. Let Uₙ=X̄, Vₙ=(1/n)ΣXᵢ² and Sₙ²=Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²/(n−1). Which statements are true?
statements: Uₙ is unbiased for θ.
Sₙ² is unbiased for θ².
Vₙ/3 is consistent for θ².
The statistic (Uₙ,Vₙ) is complete.

A.why: A Laplace distribution with location θ is symmetric about θ, so its mean is θ.

B.why: The variance of this Laplace distribution is 2θ², so the sample variance is unbiased for 2θ², not θ².

C.why: E(X²)=Var(X)+[E(X)]²=2θ²+θ²=3θ², so Vₙ/3 converges to θ².

D.why: The pair of first and second sample moments is not a complete sufficient statistic for this Laplace family.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 117 (June 2025), page 62. The supplied answer-key sheet (PDF page 65) lists statements 1 and 3, matching option B. A Laplace distribution with location θ and scale θ has mean θ and variance 2θ². Therefore Uₙ=X̄ is unbiased for θ, so A is true. The sample variance Sₙ² is unbiased for the population variance 2θ², not θ²; B is false. The second raw moment is E(X²)=Var(X)+[E(X)]²=2θ²+θ²=3θ². By the law of large numbers, Vₙ converges to 3θ², so Vₙ/3 is consistent for θ²; C is true. The pair (Uₙ,Vₙ) is not complete for this family, so D is false. Thus A and C only, option B. items.topic: inference-t4 · unbiased estimation of a finite population size from SRSWOR
items.stem: A box contains N tickets numbered 1,…,N, where N is unknown. A simple random sample of n tickets is drawn without replacement. Let X̄=(1/n)ΣXᵢ be the sample mean. Which expression is an unbiased estimator of N?
items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 96 (June 2012), page 53. The supplied answer key on page 65 lists option A. For a simple random sample without replacement from the integers 1,…,N, every population value is equally likely to be selected. The population mean is (1+N)/2. Therefore E(X̄)=(N+1)/2. Rearranging gives N=2E(X̄)−1, so E(2X̄−1)=N. Hence 2X̄−1 is unbiased for the unknown population size, option A. The scan's denominator in the displayed definition of X̄ is low-resolution and can look like capital N; it is read as n because X̄ is the sample mean of n sampled tickets, and that reading is consistent with the supplied key. items.topic: inference-t3 · Rao–Blackwell variance bound in a Poisson–binomial hierarchical model
items.stem: Let X|Y=y~Binomial(y,0.5) and Y~Poisson(λ), λ>0. Let T=T(X,Y) be any unbiased estimator of λ. Which statements are true?
statements: Var(T)≤Var(Y) for all λ.
Var(T)≥Var(Y) for all λ.
Var(T)≥λ for all λ.
Var(T)=Var(Y) for all λ.

A.why: Y itself is an unbiased estimator of λ and is complete sufficient; Rao–Blackwell/UMVU theory says no unbiased estimator can have smaller variance than Y.

B.why: Y is the UMVU estimator of λ, so every unbiased estimator T has variance at least Var(Y).

C.why: Since Y~Poisson(λ), Var(Y)=λ; statement C is equivalent to B.

D.why: An arbitrary unbiased estimator need not have the same variance as the UMVU estimator.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 79 (June 2015), page 41. The supplied answer key on page 64 lists B and C. The marginal distribution of Y is Poisson(λ), and the joint likelihood factors through Y; Y is complete sufficient for λ. Since E(Y)=λ, it is the UMVU estimator. Therefore every unbiased estimator T has Var(T)≥Var(Y)=λ. Both B and C are true. They are mathematically equivalent because Var(Y)=λ; the source lists them as separate statements, so both are retained as correct rather than treating the duplicated condition as a transcription error. A and D are false in general. items.topic: inference-t5 · method of moments and unbiased estimation in a normal mixture model
items.stem: Consider f(x;θ,σ)=0.9/σ·φ((x−θ)/σ)+0.1φ(x−θ), where θ∈R, σ>0 are unknown and φ is the standard normal density. Which statements are correct?
statements: This model is not parametric.
Method-of-moments estimators for θ and σ exist.
An unbiased estimator of θ exists.
Consistent estimators of θ do not exist.

A.why: The model is a specified two-parameter family indexed by θ and σ, so it is parametric.

B.why: The first moment gives θ, and the second central moment gives σ² through Var(X)=0.9σ²+0.1; the formal moment equations can be solved.

C.why: Both mixture components are centred at θ, so E(X)=θ and the sample mean is unbiased.

D.why: The sample mean is consistent for θ by the law of large numbers.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 80 (June 2015), page 42. The supplied answer key on page 64 lists B and C. This is a parametric family because its density is specified by the two parameters θ and σ; A is false. Both normal mixture components have mean θ, so E(X)=θ. Also Var(X)=0.9σ²+0.1, because the two components share the same mean. The first two population moments therefore provide formal method-of-moments equations: θ̂=X̄ and σ̂²=[(1/n)ΣXᵢ²−X̄²−0.1]/0.9. Thus B is true in the usual algebraic method-of-moments sense. Note that for some finite samples the computed σ̂² can be non-positive, even though the model requires σ>0; this finite-sample admissibility caveat is retained. Since E(X)=θ and the variance is finite, X̄ is unbiased and consistent for θ, proving C and showing D is false. Correct combination B and C only, option B. items.topic: inference-t3 · Bayesian estimation under squared-error loss and posterior mean
items.stem: Let X₁, X₂, X₃ be a random sample from the Uniform(0, θ) distribution. Suppose the prior distribution of θ is Uniform(0, 1). Let X₍₃₎=max{X₁, X₂, X₃}. Under squared-error loss, which of the following statements are necessarily true?
options: Statement 1 only: the Bayes estimator of θ is unique.
Statement 2 only: 1/X₍₃₎ is a Bayes estimator of θ.
Statement 3 only: X₍₃₎ is a Bayes estimator of θ.
Statement 4 only: (1−X₍₃₎)/X₍₃₎ is a Bayes estimator of θ.
items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 35 (26 November 2020), page 16. The supplied answer-key sheet on page 63 lists statements 1 and 4. We check the posterior directly because a Bayes estimator under squared-error loss is the posterior mean. Write m=X₍₃₎. For three independent Uniform(0,θ) observations, the likelihood is proportional to θ⁻³ when θ≥m and zero otherwise. The prior is uniform on (0,1), so the posterior density is proportional to θ⁻³ on m<θ<1. Its normalising integral is ∫ₘ¹θ⁻³dθ=(m⁻²−1)/2. Hence the posterior mean is [∫ₘ¹θ·θ⁻³dθ]/[(m⁻²−1)/2] = [(1/m)−1]/[(m⁻²−1)/2] = 2m/(1+m). Under squared-error loss, this posterior mean is the unique Bayes action (up to posterior-almost-sure equality). Therefore statement 1 is true. The remaining proposed expressions, 1/m, m and (1−m)/m, are not generally equal to 2m/(1+m), so statements 2, 3 and 4 are false. The mathematically supported answer is statement 1 only (option A). This conflicts with the supplied printed key (1 and 4); the discrepancy is explicitly retained rather than silently following the key. items.topic: inference-t4 · maximum likelihood with annular parameter-dependent support and parameter-space constraints
items.stem: Let (X₁,Y₁),…,(Xₙ,Yₙ) be independent observations from the uniform distribution on Sθ={(x,y): θ ≤ x²+y² ≤ θ+1}, where θ>1 is unknown. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: maxᵢ(Xᵢ²+Yᵢ²)−1 is a maximum likelihood estimate of θ.
minᵢ(Xᵢ²+Yᵢ²) is a maximum likelihood estimate of θ.
Every value between maxᵢ(Xᵢ²+Yᵢ²)−1 and minᵢ(Xᵢ²+Yᵢ²) is a maximum likelihood estimate of θ.
Every value between maxᵢXᵢ²+maxᵢYᵢ²−1 and minᵢXᵢ²+minᵢYᵢ² is a maximum likelihood estimate of θ.
items.explanation: Write Rᵢ=Xᵢ²+Yᵢ², Rmin=minᵢRᵢ and Rmax=maxᵢRᵢ. The annulus Sθ has area π[(θ+1)−θ]=π, so the joint likelihood is π⁻ⁿ when every observation satisfies θ≤Rᵢ≤θ+1, and is zero otherwise. Therefore the likelihood is positive exactly for θ in [Rmax−1,Rmin]∩(1,∞). For a sample drawn from this model, there is a true θ₀>1 with θ₀≤Rᵢ≤θ₀+1. Hence Rmin>1 and Rmax−Rmin≤1. Taking θ=Rmin is always admissible: it is greater than 1 and Rmax≤Rmin+1. Thus statement 2 is always an MLE. Statement 1 is not guaranteed because Rmax−1 can be ≤1, outside the parameter space. Statement 3 is not guaranteed because the interval can include values ≤1. Statement 4 uses separate coordinatewise extrema and does not describe the radial support condition. The supplied answer key on source page 63 lists statement 1 only; that conflicts with the parameter restriction θ>1 and the likelihood calculation. We retain the mathematically valid result, statement 2, and explicitly flag the printed-key discrepancy rather than silently reproducing it. Source: supplied Estimation CSIR NET PDF, page 7 (Q16, February 2022); answer key page 63. items.topic: inference-t4 · unbiasedness and consistency of scale estimators under a normal model
items.stem: Consider a sequence of i.i.d. observations X₁,X₂,… from N(0,σ²). Which of the following are unbiased and consistent estimators of σ?
items.explanation: For X∼N(0,σ²), the absolute value has a half-normal distribution and E|X|=σ√(2/π). Therefore E[√(π/2)|X|]=σ, and by linearity E[√(π/2)(1/n)Σ|Xᵢ|]=σ. This proves option A is unbiased. By the strong law of large numbers, (1/n)Σ|Xᵢ| converges almost surely to E|X|=σ√(2/π), so the scaled estimator converges almost surely to σ; it is consistent as well. Option B is the root mean square. It converges to σ by the law of large numbers, but for finite n its expectation is strictly less than √E(X²)=σ by Jensen's inequality (the square-root function is strictly concave and the sample mean of squares is non-degenerate), so it is biased. Option C is the usual sample standard deviation; it is consistent, but is not unbiased for σ (the unbiased estimator is the sample variance for σ², not its square root for σ). Option D depends only on X₁ and Xₙ; as n grows it does not average an increasing number of independent observations and its distribution does not concentrate at σ, so it is not consistent. The supplied answer key on source page 63 lists option 1, agreeing with the derivation. Source: supplied Estimation CSIR NET PDF, page 8 (Q19, February 2022); answer key page 63.
